lesson.title: Beyond the Brain: Mapping the Peripheral Nervous System
lesson.summary: This section introduces the peripheral nervous system, the network of nerves that connects the brain and spinal cord to the rest of the body, and its two main subdivisions.
lesson.body:
The nervous system as a whole divides into two major parts. The central nervous system, made up of the brain and spinal cord, functions as the body's command center, processing information and generating decisions. On its own, however, the central nervous system has no direct way to sense the outside world or move a muscle. That job belongs to the peripheral nervous system, the vast network of nerves that lies outside the brain and spinal cord and physically connects the central nervous system to every muscle, gland, and sensory receptor throughout the body.

The peripheral nervous system carries information in two directions at once, much like a highway system connecting a capital city to every town in a country. Sensory, or afferent, neurons carry information inward, from the eyes, skin, muscles, and internal organs toward the brain and spinal cord, which is how the central nervous system learns anything about the state of the body and the outside world in the first place. Motor, or efferent, neurons carry information outward, from the central nervous system to muscles and glands, which is how decisions made in the brain actually turn into movement or physiological change. Without this two way traffic, the central nervous system would be permanently cut off, unable to sense anything or act on anything.

The peripheral nervous system itself splits into two further subdivisions based on the kind of activity it controls. The somatic nervous system governs voluntary movement of the skeletal muscles, the kind of movement you consciously choose to make, such as reaching for a cup, and also relays sensory information from the skin, muscles, and joints back to the central nervous system. The autonomic nervous system, by contrast, governs the involuntary activity of internal organs, things like heart rate and digestion that happen automatically without conscious control. This second subdivision is important enough that it gets its own full discussion in the next section.

A simple reflex helps make this whole system concrete. Touch a hot stove by accident, and sensory neurons in the peripheral nervous system immediately carry that pain signal inward toward the spinal cord. Motor neurons in the peripheral nervous system then carry the command back outward to the muscles of your arm, snapping your hand away, and this reflex arc is actually coordinated at the level of the spinal cord fast enough that your hand often pulls back before your brain has even finished consciously registering the pain.

None of this would be possible without the central nervous system covered previously, since the peripheral nervous system exists specifically to serve it, carrying the raw sensory material the brain needs to work with and carrying out the decisions the brain and spinal cord make. The two systems function only as a connected whole, never independently of each other.
